intro.html: “Happy” is a fine word, but it does a lot of jobs. Is the happiness loud or quiet? Sudden or steady? Earned by a victory, or simply part of someone’s nature? The ten words in this topic each name a different kind of joy, and choosing the right one lets a reader hear the cheering, see the bouncing or feel the calm hope.

A burst of joy: elated (thrilled by good news), jubilant (joy at a win), ecstatic and euphoric (overwhelming happiness). A happy nature: buoyant (bounces back), blithe (carefree, maybe too carefree), ebullient and exuberant (bubbling with energy), sanguine (hopeful). The sound of it: mirth (laughter and fun).

words.def: very happy and excited about something good
words.ex: Maya was {elated} when the letter said she had made the team.
words.ctx: After months of rejection letters, the young writer was {elated}: a magazine had finally accepted her story and planned to print it in the spring issue.
words.etym: From Latin elatus, “lifted up,” a form of efferre, “to carry out, to raise.”

mn.cue: e-LAY-ted: she LAID a golden egg!
mn.text: Henrietta the hen has just laid a golden egg, and she flaps and clucks with joy. She is {elated}.

scene.alt: A joyful hen stands by the golden egg she has just laid while a boy cheers.

words.def: joyful and triumphant, especially after a success
words.ex: The {jubilant} fans poured onto the field after the final whistle.
words.ctx: The mood in the gym was {jubilant}: the team had just won its first championship in forty years, and nobody wanted to go home.
words.etym: From Latin jubilare, “to shout for joy.”

mn.cue: JUBIL-ANTS: the Ants won the cup!
mn.text: The Ants, the smallest team in the league, just won the cup, and every player is leaping and cheering. They are {jubilant}.

scene.alt: Three players on a team called the Ants leap and cheer, holding up a trophy.

words.ex: The puppy was {ecstatic} to see its family come home after a week away.
words.ctx: Lila had expected socks for her birthday, so when she unwrapped a telescope, she was {ecstatic}, shrieking and hugging everyone in the room.
words.etym: From Greek ekstatikos, from ekstasis, “standing outside oneself”: ek (out) + histanai (to place, to stand).

mn.text: Ivy is so happy about her new puppy that she crackles like static electricity: she jumps, squeals and sparks with joy. She is {ecstatic}.

scene.alt: A girl leaps with joy, sparks flying, as a puppy jumps up to greet her.

words.ex: The {euphoric} climbers hugged and took pictures on the summit.
words.ctx: Crossing the finish line of her first marathon, Tia felt {euphoric}: the ache in her legs vanished, and she laughed and cried at the same time.
words.etym: From Greek euphoria, “well-being,” from euphoros, “bearing well”: eu (well) + pherein (to bear).

mn.text: Tia finishes her first marathon and feels so light with joy that she could float off into the sky like a UFO. She is {euphoric}.

scene.alt: A runner with a medal floats up among the clouds, glowing with happiness.

words.def: cheerful and hopeful; also, able to float
words.ex: Despite the rain, the campers stayed {buoyant}, singing all the way back to their cabins.
words.ctx: The team had lost its first three games, yet the players remained {buoyant}, joking at practice and sure that their luck was about to turn.
words.etym: Probably from Spanish boyante, “floating,” from boya, buoy.

mn.cue: BUOY-ant: bobs up like a BUOY
mn.text: A wave knocks Sven’s hat into the sea, and he just laughs and bobs along like a buoy. His spirits always float back up: he is {buoyant}.

scene.alt: A man in a rowboat laughs as the wind blows his hat away; a life ring bobs nearby.

words.def: cheerful and carefree, sometimes carelessly so
words.ex: Humming a {blithe} tune, Zoe skipped down the lane to the pond.
words.ctx: His {blithe} attitude toward deadlines worried his teammates; he whistled and joked while the project sat unfinished the night before it was due.
words.etym: From Old English blithe, “joyful,” related to bliss.
words.note: Blithe can be praise (a blithe spirit) or blame (a blithe disregard for the rules): carefree cheer in the wrong place is carelessness.

mn.text: Pip skips home whistling, blissful and light as a feather, without a care in the world, not even for the storm cloud right behind him. He is {blithe}.

scene.alt: A boy skips and whistles happily, not noticing a rain cloud behind him.

words.ex: The {ebullient} host greeted every guest with a hug and a joke.
words.ctx: Usually quiet, Professor Edwin became {ebullient} whenever someone asked about dinosaurs, waving his arms and talking faster than anyone could take notes.
words.etym: From Latin ebullire, “to boil up”: e (out) + bullire (to bubble, to boil).

mn.text: Like a pot bubbling over, Zoe can’t hold in her joy at her first A: she jumps, laughs and hugs the whole class. She is {ebullient}.

scene.alt: A girl leaps for joy with her graded paper while a classmate claps.

words.def: full of energy, excitement and joy
words.ex: The {exuberant} puppy raced around the yard, leaping at every leaf.
words.ctx: The concert hall was usually hushed, but tonight the crowd was {exuberant}, clapping along, dancing in the aisles and calling for one more song.
words.etym: From Latin exuberare, “to be abundantly fruitful,” from uber, “fertile.”

mn.cue: ex-ZOO-ber-ant: a ZOO bursting with joy
mn.text: The keeper rolls in a birthday cake, and the whole zoo bursts with joy: the monkey leaps, the parrot sings, the elephant sprays a happy fountain. The animals are {exuberant}.

scene.alt: An elephant, a leaping monkey and a singing parrot celebrate around a birthday cake.

words.ex: The puppet show filled the library with {mirth}.
words.ctx: The meeting had been tense, but when the principal’s puppy trotted in wearing a party hat, the room dissolved into {mirth}; even the grumpiest teacher laughed.
words.etym: From Old English myrgth, related to merry.

mn.text: At Theo’s birthday party, the puppy steals the party hat and wears it, and the whole room bursts into laughter. Birthdays bring {mirth}.

scene.alt: Children in party hats laugh as a puppy wears a hat at a birthday party.

words.def: hopeful and confident about the future
words.ex: Despite the gray sky, Dad was {sanguine} about our chances for a beach day.
words.ctx: The rest of the crew doubted the old boat would ever float again, but Sven remained {sanguine}, sure that a little paint and patience would have her sailing by summer.
words.etym: From Latin sanguineus, “of blood”; doctors of the Middle Ages believed a hopeful, cheerful temper came from plenty of blood.

mn.text: The sky is gray, but Jamal wears a sun grin and packs the beach umbrella anyway: “It’ll clear up by noon!” He is {sanguine}.

scene.alt: Under a gray cloud, a grinning man in sunglasses points to the sun peeking out.

after.cap: Kinds of happiness: a moment, a nature or a hope.

after.html: sanguine comes from the Latin word for blood, but in English it means hopeful. blithe can be a warning: a blithe disregard for danger is carelessness, not cheer.

items.q: The coach is sanguine about Saturday’s game. How does she feel?
choices: hopeful that the team will do well
items.why: Sanguine means hopeful and confident about the future, even though it comes from the Latin word for blood.

items.q: Which sentence uses blithe as a criticism?
choices: He showed a blithe disregard for the warning signs and kept hiking toward the storm.
Her blithe song cheered up the whole bus.
The blithe puppy bounded across the lawn.
items.why: Ignoring danger cheerfully is blithe in the bad sense: carefree to the point of carelessness.

items.q: True or false: mirth is an adjective meaning funny.
items.why: False. Mirth is a noun: laughter and amusement. The adjective is mirthful.

items.q: Which word best fits fans celebrating a championship win?
items.why: Jubilant is joy at a success or victory; the fans are cheering a win.
